note: Two instantiations per unit, one in baking and one in carpentry. copied_runs is the longest shared content-word run against the whole paper.

instantiations: Every morning, home bakers mix and shape dough with a goal to keep a steady weekly loaf.
Every morning, woodworkers cut and fit boards with a goal to keep a steady weekly frame.
Rye dough is a stubborn mix and does not rise the way wheat does. However, it keeps well on the counter.
Pine is a soft timber and does not hold a screw the way oak does. However, it planes cleanly.
By comparison, wheat dough is forgiving, often used when a bake has to be reliable, but it dries out fast if left uncovered - it skins over within the hour.
By comparison, oak is stable, often used when a joint has to stay tight, but it blunts edges quickly - a plane iron dulls after a few passes.
Our kitchen was asked by a neighbor to work out a weekly bake, using only the dough already on the bench, that decides each morning's folds.
Our shop was asked by a neighbor to work out a weekly build, using only the boards already in the rack, that decides each morning's cuts.
Home bakers mix and shape dough hoping for a taller loaf. The kitchen was asked for a weekly bake so that the family eats well.
Woodworkers cut and fit boards hoping for a stiffer frame. The shop was asked for a weekly build so that the order stands square.
We have settled on a weekly bake that picks the morning to start, using dough already on hand, that allows for the flour we lose to the bench and keeps the wheat and the rye in balance.
We have settled on a weekly build that picks the morning to start, using boards already on hand, that allows for the timber we lose to the saw and keeps the oak and the pine in balance.
Although the dough log has gaps, it serves the bake well as we only read the dough once a morning.
Although the board tally has gaps, it serves the build well as we only read the boards once a morning.
We lean on two old baking habits and fold them into one weekly plan.
We lean on two old shop habits and fold them into one weekly plan.
We add, deliberately, a small correction for the cold tin.
We add, deliberately, a small correction for the damp rack.
This correction stops a false reading that could push the bake toward a sunk loaf.
This correction stops a false reading that could push the build toward a loose joint.
Over and above the plan for an ordinary week, we add a rule that wakes up when a dough collapses and outranks the ordinary plan.
Over and above the plan for an ordinary week, we add a rule that wakes up when a board splits and outranks the ordinary plan.
The main strength of the bake is that it draws on a sound mix of habits, which keeps us clear of the usual ruined batches.
The main strength of the build is that it draws on a sound mix of habits, which keeps us clear of the usual ruined joints.
It shrugs off small changes that a fussier bake might turn to advantage, and prefers to wait for a clear rise.
It shrugs off small changes that a fussier build might turn to advantage, and prefers to wait for a clear fit.
Notes: long rest, window pane, poke test, cold proof, bench flour, morning start.
Notes: long dry-fit, knock test, flex test, cold glue, sawdust, morning start.
Baking is a matter of timing.
Joinery is a matter of fit.
It is easy to look back at a finished loaf and see where the dough went wrong, but calling the moment to bake ahead of time is a plainly harder thing.
It is easy to look back at a finished frame and see where the joint went wrong, but calling the moment to glue ahead of time is a plainly harder thing.

On top of that, new flours turn up at the mill often and behave differently, so each one wants its own handling. To make matters worse, home baking from a written log is fairly recent, and there are only a few seasons of notes.

On top of that, new timbers turn up at the yard often and behave differently, so each one wants its own handling. To make matters worse, hand work from a written log is fairly recent, and there are only a few seasons of notes.
Set against a lifetime of baking, one season of notes is a short record and it is hard to read a habit from that by itself.
Set against a lifetime of woodwork, one season of notes is a short record and it is hard to read a habit from that by itself.
For this kitchen we have wheat, rye, and starter. We have no old notes when the first week begins. Every bake costs flour. The job is to feed the family.
For this shop we have oak, pine, and offcuts. We have no old notes when the first week begins. Every joint costs timber. The job is to fill the order.
We settled on watching the dough and answering it.
We settled on watching the board and answering it.
Fold: working the dough by turning it over and adding the flour that sticks to the bench.
Cut: working the board by passing it through the saw and adding the kerf the blade takes.
Starter: in this kitchen, starter means the jar kept on the top shelf.
Offcuts: in this shop, offcuts means the short pieces kept under the bench.
We make a handful of assumptions in this bake to keep the planning simple.
We make a handful of assumptions in this build to keep the planning simple.
Claim: the dough will keep rising and falling through the week. Reason: without that rise and fall there is nothing to bake for.
Claim: the boards will keep moving through the season. Reason: without that movement there is nothing to fit for.
A dead starter or a collapsed tin. Both are very rare.
A split board or a sprung joint. Both are very rare.
This is a capped-loss rule: if the dough sits flat all week, the kitchen loses the flour, nothing beyond that.
This is a capped-loss rule: if the boards sit still all season, the shop loses the offcuts, nothing beyond that.
The two sketches show how the dough behaved across the week. Although the two flours look alike, the second sketch shows the difference in rise is large.
The two sketches show how the boards behaved across the season. Although the two timbers look alike, the second sketch shows the difference in movement is large.
The plan is joined up; this means it knows about the other loaves and will not start two bakes that fight each other.
The plan is joined up; this means it knows about the other frames and will not start two glue-ups that fight each other.
Reading the spring of a dough is a quick check.
Reading the flex of a board is a quick check.
The rise, or the height gained since the last fold.
The flex, or the gap closed since the last pass.
Where the mark is the poke of that morning and the height is the same as before.
Where the mark is the knock of that morning and the width is the same as before.
If the dough springs past the line and sits above its usual height, a bake is called and stays called until the next morning. Otherwise, we wait.
If the board closes past the line and sits under its usual width, a glue-up is called and stays called until the next morning. Otherwise, we wait.
A long rest is a sound habit when the dough climbs past its usual height. We also want the bake to notice a dough that sags below that height, and so we add a second habit.
A long dry-fit is a sound habit when the board closes past its usual width. We also want the build to notice a board that opens below that width, and so we add a second habit.
For our kitchen, this says that the further a dough sags, the more likely the next morning brings it back. Read loosely, a sag tends to correct itself.
For our shop, this says that the further a board opens, the more likely the next morning brings it back. Read loosely, a gap tends to correct itself.
For the long rest, we say that the promise of a loaf grows with the spring of the dough.
For the long dry-fit, we say that the promise of a frame grows with the closing of the joint.
Our rule for pulling a loaf is plain and cautious.
Our rule for pulling a joint is plain and cautious.
If the tin smells done, the loaf comes out.
If the joint closes tight, the clamp comes off.
This rules out pulling a loaf too early, as would happen if the kitchen used its ordinary morning check.
This rules out pulling a joint too early, as would happen if the shop used its ordinary morning check.
The kitchen then keeps its hands off that dough for some mornings.
The shop then keeps its hands off that board for some mornings.
The reason is wasted flour: folding and baking at every small change can look very rewarding, but the flour lost to the bench starts to eat the week's loaves.
The reason is wasted timber: cutting and regluing at every small change can look very rewarding, but the timber lost to the saw starts to eat the week's frames.
If the week turns bad, the work moves to the bad-week rule and the rest of the morning is skipped.
If the season turns bad, the work moves to the bad-week rule and the rest of the morning is skipped.
We deal with the cold tin by adding a correction that behaves like a smaller fold on a colder morning.
We deal with the damp rack by adding a correction that behaves like a lighter pass on a damper morning.
The sketch shows how the week finished. The rack ends full.
The sketch shows how the season finished. The order ends full.
Look at mornings three, seven, and twelve.
Look at mornings three, seven, and twelve.
The bake is meant to feed the family. So it gives up the safe rye loaf in favor of committing the whole bench to wheat when the rise is strong.
The build is meant to fill the order. So it gives up the safe pine frame in favor of committing the whole rack to oak when the fit is tight.
On the way up the two bakes track each other closely. On the way down, though, ours holds far steadier.
On the way closed the two builds track each other closely. On the way open, though, ours holds far steadier.
The vertical line is a plain tally of loaves, with no unit attached.
The vertical line is a plain tally of frames, with no unit attached.
Look at the tall marks in the first few mornings. This comes from having almost nothing written down yet, since the bake can only use mornings it has already seen.
Look at the tall marks in the first few mornings. This comes from having almost nothing written down yet, since the build can only use mornings it has already seen.
Early on there is no record to compare against, and so the bake reads a small rise as a big one. That is why the first mornings still produce loaves.
Early on there is no record to compare against, and so the build reads a small closing as a big one. That is why the first mornings still produce frames.
In the chart below, the row marked finest is a judgment we wrote in by hand, not a count.
In the chart below, the row marked finest is a judgment we wrote in by hand, not a count.
The bake gives fewer loaves as the flour lost to the bench grows, as one would expect.
The build gives fewer frames as the timber lost to the saw grows, as one would expect.
Because the loss is a share of the dough, it stays small when the week is quiet. In a week of fast rises, though, a small early loss compounds.
Because the loss is a share of the board, it stays small when the season is quiet. In a season of fast closings, though, a small early loss compounds.
We can check the bake by watching which mornings a loaf went in.
We can check the build by watching which mornings a joint was glued.
On morning four of that week (morning forty of the whole run), the bake senses a sag and waits.
On morning four of that week (morning forty of the whole run), the build senses an opening and waits.
Although this makes the bake miss the peak by a little, the loaf is still very good.
Although this makes the build miss the tightest fit by a little, the frame is still very good.
See the empty stretch from morning four to morning nine. That is the hands-off rule switching on after a bake.
See the empty stretch from morning four to morning nine. That is the hands-off rule switching on after a glue-up.
This is precisely the week we were hoping for
This is precisely the season we were hoping for
We look at a different stretch of mornings because later on the wheat signals crowd out the rye and the rye tells us nothing.
We look at a different stretch of mornings because later on the oak signals crowd out the pine and the pine tells us nothing.
The sketch marks the mornings a loaf went in, but not how much dough.
The sketch marks the mornings a joint was glued, but not how much timber.

When the dough sits quiet, wandering between two heights, the bake follows its ordinary habit and still produces loaves. If the dough breaks upward and climbs fast, the bake spots it at once and switches habit.

When the board sits quiet, wandering between two widths, the build follows its ordinary habit and still produces frames. If the board breaks closed and tightens fast, the build spots it at once and switches habit.
The bake also does well with little or no old record, being built entirely on habit. Yet it does change as the weeks pass, taking in the recent rests and the recent rises.
The build also does well with little or no old record, being built entirely on habit. Yet it does change as the weeks pass, taking in the recent fits and the recent closings.
Even so, the sketch shows that for small changes in the morning routine the drop in loaves is modest.
Even so, the sketch shows that for small changes in the morning routine the drop in frames is modest.
Although it is nowhere near the best week we can imagine, the bake still feeds the family most weeks.
Although it is nowhere near the best season we can imagine, the build still fills the order most weeks.
For a lively dough, it is hard to say whether answering every small change is a fault or a virtue.
For a lively board, it is hard to say whether answering every small change is a fault or a virtue.

To manage that, we had to write a plan that could run on a very short record. We used a long rest together with a sag-correcting habit. We then extended the plan with a rule for bad weeks. Tuning the plan showed us the morning routine that suited it.

To manage that, we had to write a plan that could run on a very short record. We used a long dry-fit together with a gap-correcting habit. We then extended the plan with a rule for bad weeks. Tuning the plan showed us the morning routine that suited it.
Our bake held up well on the flours we had and came out ahead of the usual weekly loaf, turning one sack into a full rack.
Our build held up well on the timbers we had and came out ahead of the usual weekly frame, turning one stack into a full order.
Our kitchen was given the job of working out the best morning to bake.
Our shop was given the job of working out the best morning to glue.

The pace of a bake is read from the spring - how much the dough climbs between one fold and the next - and from the running height - the recent pokes added up and divided by how many mornings they cover.

The pace of a build is read from the closing - how much the joint tightens between one pass and the next - and from the running width - the recent knocks added up and divided by how many mornings they cover.
The second part of the morning is deciding how much dough goes into the tin.
The second part of the morning is deciding how much timber goes into the clamp.

After running the build across the season, we ended with a full order - a very large return on the first stack.
Though the bake feeds the family and runs smoothly, we see what it does well and where it falls short. We would be glad to talk over any further ideas for improving it.
Though the build fills the order and runs smoothly, we see what it does well and where it falls short. We would be glad to talk over any further ideas for improving it.

The routes are: prove the dough overnight, or answer it the moment it slumps. What that second route still owes: when to stop the fold, when to stop the bake, how much of each flour, a collapse mid-proof, rises of different sizes, a dusty bench.

The routes are: thickness the whole frame first, or answer each joint the moment it gaps. What that second route still owes: when to stop the cut, when to stop the glue, how much of each board, a split mid-clamp, gaps of different sizes, a dusty bench.
